subject: Katz v. United States (1967) and the birth of the 'reasonable expectation of privacy' — the Fourth Amendment moves from protecting places to protecting people
central_question: If the police never touch your property — never break in, never trespass — but a hidden microphone captures your private words out of the open air, is that a 'search' the Constitution controls?
viewer_promise: By the end, the viewer understands how a single 1967 Supreme Court decision moved the Fourth Amendment from guarding physical places to guarding people, why recording a man in a glass phone booth without ever touching it was ruled an unconstitutional search, and where the 'reasonable expectation of privacy' test that now governs modern surveillance actually came from.
surprise: Federal agents recorded a suspect's phone calls without ever setting foot inside the booth or breaking any physical barrier — exactly the kind of no-trespass surveillance the law had long said was fair game — and the Supreme Court still ruled it an illegal search, tearing up a forty-year-old rule in the process.
stakes: Whether the government needs a warrant before secretly listening to your private conversations, and how a case about a bookmaker in a phone booth became the legal foundation for privacy in the age of wiretaps, cell phones, and digital surveillance.
target_audience: English-speaking US general audience interested in law, policing, privacy, technology and how systems work
demand_evidence: 'Know your rights,' privacy, and surveillance content is a large, durable YouTube genre; Katz is the origin point of the modern 'expectation of privacy' idea that every wiretap and phone-search story rests on.
Landmark-case explainers sustain long-tail search interest, and Katz is the case courts and commentators cite whenever a new form of eavesdropping appears.
competition: Most existing videos recite the 'people, not places' line or fold Katz into a general Fourth Amendment survey; few center the causal story of how the old trespass rule fell and how a mere concurrence became the governing test.
differentiation: Frames Katz as the exact moment the Court cut the Fourth Amendment loose from physical trespass and re-anchored it to people, present-tense and self-relevant, with primary-source citations and a neutral, advertiser-safe tone. Direct sequel to the Kyllo episode: Kyllo protected the home by its walls; Katz protects the person even in a glass box on a public sidewalk.
research_feasibility: High: the opinion is public domain (389 U.S. 347); Cornell LII, Justia and Oyez provide the full majority opinion, concurrences, dissent and case record.
visual_feasibility: High: a lone glowing 1960s glass phone booth on a night street, a hidden microphone and reel-to-reel recorder, escaping sound-waves, a 'places vs. people' motif, a 7-1 split, and a modern-surveillance tie (smartphones, data streams).
risk_notes: Decided landmark case (1967); opinion is public domain - advertiser-friendly.
Gambling-adjacent subject: the illegal wagering is treated only as the factual court record and the reason for the surveillance; no how-to, no glamorization, no depiction of betting.
Charles (Charlie) Katz and the justices are real people on the public record; treat respectfully and factually, by role; no real-person likeness in AI visuals (invariant 11).

Keep tone neutral between personal privacy and legitimate law-enforcement need. Do NOT overstate the holding: the Court did NOT ban wiretapping or electronic surveillance; it required prior judicial authorization (a warrant).
Present the 'reasonable expectation of privacy' test as Justice Harlan's concurrence that later became the standard, NOT as the words of the majority holding.
Generated visuals are illustration/reconstruction, never presented as authentic surveillance or archival footage.
kill_conditions: Cannot source the holding and key facts to the primary opinion (389 U.S. 347) plus one independent reference.
